## Chapter 73: Design of Experiments

### When Analysis Can Happen With Existing Data

Sometimes, enough data already exists, or enough change already exists within the current process, that a Six Sigma team can make decisions about factors without running a designed experiment. In those cases, the data is already available, or can be captured in a way that isolates several inputs, so a Six Sigma team can run analysis and hypothesis tests without recreating physical scenarios. For example, in an agricultural setting, a company might already be using several types of planting processes to grow the same crop. Teams could gather data on each type of planting process, make sure no other variables exist between those processes, and then draw valid conclusions about how the planting processes impact harvest outcomes.

There are benefits and downsides to analyzing existing data instead of running a designed experiment. The first benefit is that basing the primary analysis and initial solution selection on existing data typically shortens the timeline of the entire DMAIC process. A team might still have to pilot a solution, measuring and analyzing the results to make sure they match the initial predictions, but it doesn't need to implement a designed experiment to make those first predictions. Second, basing decisions on existing data or processes can lower a DMAIC project's overall cost. This is especially true for processes involving machines or parts that would have to be reconfigured to create a change in some inputs. In some cases, it's simply not possible to make such changes just so a team can gather information to base such conclusions on, and the Six Sigma practitioner needs to use other tools to analyze the process, so the team can draw conclusions and suggest improvements for a more formal pilot or test.

The downside of using existing data is that it isn't always clean. You might use existing data on a process when a process includes multiple changes in a factor. You'd even run the same analysis you'd run if you'd made those changes yourself as part of an experiment. The problem is that you have no control over the other variables in the process. For example, a Six Sigma team might be working on how document printing is managed at a large law firm. The team wants to know whether the copy-and-print station documents are sent to impacts how fast jobs get processed. The copy-and-print machines have internal logs that record when a job is received and when it finished printing, so the team can compare process speed across all stations using ANOVA or DOE analysis without actually designing and running an experiment. The team could simply pull historical process data from last week — or from any given period.

What isn't logged for the copy-and-print process is a variety of external factors, including how many employees were working at a given moment, whether the machines went through maintenance needs or paper jams, and whether employees were interrupting print jobs to handle copying, scanning, or faxing on the same machines. While historical data can provide valuable information about each machine's productivity difference, the team might not be able to rule out some of these other factors as the cause without a designed experiment that captures all possibly relevant data.

### Why Run an Experiment?

A well-designed experiment helps you understand which variables provide the most influence over the process outcome. That helps a Six Sigma team understand where time, money, and other resources should be spent. In the example above, the experiment can help the team rule out external factors and understand whether the copy-and-print station's type or location is an important factor in productivity.

Another reason to run an experiment is that it can help you understand how to set inputs to create the best possible outcome. In one of this book's earlier chapters, we used the example of a manufacturing process that produces chocolate bars. Each of the inputs — the ingredient amounts, mixing time, and mixing temperature — has to be set at the right level to create an optimal product. A Six Sigma team working on that process might run experiments to test various input levels, in order to find the right combination for the desired outcome.

Sometimes, Six Sigma teams want to understand how to control or set inputs that are simply influential to a process, but don't necessarily directly feed the outcome. In the chocolate bar example, if the team found optimal settings for the ingredients, time, and mixing temperature, and still sees variation in the process outcome, it might then consider influential inputs. Does room temperature influence the chocolate's mixing and hardening process? If the team decides it might be influential, it could run an experiment testing various room temperatures to find the right level for the best process outcome.

Finally, not every input is under a Six Sigma team's or the process owner's control. You can control the temperature in a climate-controlled room, but you can't control the outdoor temperature, for example. Experiments can help teams understand how to set every input they can control, to reduce any impact on variation and outcome coming from inputs they can't control.

### Best-Guess Trial and Error versus Factorial Experiments

A designed experiment is exactly that — it's statistically designed to test a variety of factors. While a designed experiment has trial and error at its base, teams using design of experiments aren't simply making their best possible guess about the question. A best-guess trial-and-error approach isn't actually efficient in most cases, even though some people might think otherwise.

To better understand the difference between a designed experiment and a best-guess approach, consider a real-world application. A team is working to improve a process at a regional furniture warehouse that delivers furniture to retail stores based on weekly store orders. The team wants to cut the average delivery time by 24 hours and has the baseline measurement — the current average order-delivery time is 72 hours.

Using a best-guess approach, the team would identify what it thinks is the combination of inputs most likely to impact delivery times. The team might decide the factors include the delivery driver, the dispatcher who provides instructions and directions, whether the driver has GPS in the truck, and how many pieces of furniture are being delivered. To figure out which factor contributes most to delivery time, or find out which factors could be changed to lower average times, the team would then have to run a series of trial-and-error tests.

The team sets the factors and runs one scenario. If the delivery time is greater than 48 hours, the outcome isn't the desired one. The team changes one of the factors and runs the test again. The team has to repeat the process until it finds the magic combination. Not only is this inefficient, it uses an approach called OFAT, or One-Factor-At-a-Time. Only one input setting is changed per test, and one measurement is taken. The measurements are compared to make decisions about each factor. In the furniture example, the team might notice that delivery times are faster when there's GPS on board the truck. It might also notice that delivery times are faster when there's a more experienced driver on board the truck, regardless of GPS presence.

One of the main problems with testing one factor at a time — besides the inefficiency — is that Six Sigma practitioners don't get a true understanding of the interaction between the changes. Yes, having a GPS increases efficiency. Yes, having an experienced driver increases efficiency. But what happens when both a GPS and an experienced driver are on board a truck? Does efficiency increase at some exponential level, or does it simply rise to the maximum value between the experience-related increase or the GPS-related increase? Likewise, what happens when a negative factor is combined with a positive one? If delivery times increase with every item added to the order, what happens to the impact of driver experience on efficiency? One-factor-at-a-time approaches generally don't answer these questions.

### Why Do People Think This Is a Good Approach?

Based on the scenario above, you can see that the best-guess approach is labor-intensive and time-consuming. The problem is that many people within an organization often prefer this approach because it's already worked well before. If you're very familiar with a process, you can get a good result right off the first few guesses. In our furniture-moving example, you don't even need to be extremely familiar with the process to guess that having GPS on board every delivery truck likely reduces delivery times, or that it'll take longer to deliver more furniture.

Because of the tendency to favor a best-guess approach, Six Sigma practitioners may have to work to explain the importance of using statistical analysis to help with problem-solving. It's important for teams to understand that a best-guess approach usually leads to more tests and attempts than necessary, which creates waste, or muda. Yes, teams can get lucky, especially if someone on the team or a subject-matter expert used by the team is extremely familiar with the process and thus understands how the inputs impact outcomes at a granular level. However, that familiarity with the process can create the opposite impact. The person might be so close to the process, and so set in the traditional way of doing things, that they can't make good guesses.

Even if the first guess about input changes produces an outcome within the parameters the team was seeking, it might not be the best possible guess. The team in the delivery example wanted to cut delivery times by an average of 24 hours. Based on historical data, any combination of inputs averaging 48 hours or less would achieve that goal. But what if there's a combination of inputs averaging 24 hours or less? Wouldn't that be valuable for the team to know? If the input combination is feasible to achieve, then the team wouldn't just meet the original goal — it would deliver well beyond the original goal. That's not something teams should always aim to do, because setting the bar too high can have negative results on a project. But knowing that excellent outcomes are possible is valuable, because it lets the team make a more educated decision about the solution.

### What Is Factorial Experimentation?

The solution to all the inefficiency and uninformative-data problems described above is design of experiments, or factorial experimentation. Design of experiments is also called statistically designed experiments, and it involves running a series of experimental runs that vary all the input factors in an organized way. The information isn't analyzed until all the planned runs are complete, meaning you have all the data from all the input changes at that point.

For example, consider again the factors from the furniture-delivery example: number of pieces being delivered, driver experience, whether GPS is on board, and the dispatcher's method for providing instructions or directions. For this example, assume each of those factors can be set at a low value and a high value, as follows.

- Driver experience: 0 years, 1 year
- GPS: No, Yes
- Dispatcher: No policy, follows a policy
- Number of furniture pieces: 1, 5

On a grid, you'd build a list of every possible run. Each run creates a unique grouping of the possible factors, meaning the number of runs you have is determined by the number of factors and possible settings you have. The grid for the delivery factors is shown below.

*(Table: a grid of 16 runs combining Driver Experience (0/1 year), GPS (Yes/No), Dispatcher (follows/doesn't follow procedure), and Pieces of Furniture (1/5 pieces) — all 16 possible combinations of a 2⁴ factorial design.)*

That information is then used to generate a worksheet for running the experiment; once data is collected, a Six Sigma practitioner analyzes the outcome. Minitab actually has tools that help you build the worksheet and analyze the experiment's outcome, which we'll cover at the end of this chapter and in the next.

Notice that the experiment above is an example of a designed 2^k factorial experiment. In a 2^k factorial design, you limit the factor levels to two: a high and a low. The driver has less than one year (0 years) of experience, or 1 year or more of experience. GPS is either present or it isn't.

Experiments that include more than two levels — more than one low and one high — for one or more factors are full factorial experiments. This chapter's examples all deal with 2^k factorials; examples of full factorials can be found in Chapter 74.

### Step-by-Step Guide to Building a Designed Experiment

Just as with hypothesis testing, most experiments follow a roadmap of steps needed to define the elements, set up data collection, and analyze the collected data. These steps are nearly the same for any type of experiment, although you'll see in Chapter 74 that some requirements differ slightly when dealing with full factorials.

**Step 1: In practical or business terms, what's the problem?**

As with anything in Six Sigma, you start with a practical business consideration or question. This isn't necessarily the big problem statement the team built during the project's Define phase. It's more likely a smaller question within the bigger problem. For example, a healthcare facility might want to address the staph infection rate in inpatients. That might be the team's overall project: reduce the current staph infection rate, which is 17 percent.

During the project, the team finds that the clinical staff doesn't always follow sanitization protocols when treating patients. For this specific situation, the practical problem might be stated as: on a 10-point sanitization compliance assessment, clinical healthcare professionals average 7.1. The hospital requires an average of at least 9.0.

The business problem or concern the experiment is addressing needs to tie back to the Six Sigma team's overall problem statement. In this case, the lack of sanitization compliance might be linked to the fact that patients are contracting staph infections.

**Step 2: What's the goal of running a designed experiment?**

Unlike some of the other analyses discussed in this book, designed experiments often consume the time and resources of someone besides the Six Sigma practitioner, meaning there's a higher cost associated with DOE than there might be with graphical analysis or even hypothesis testing. Because of that, teams don't want to run experiments without a detailed goal — a detailed understanding of why the experiment is needed and what the team hopes to achieve through the analysis.

The goal is directly tied to the practical problem. In the healthcare example, the problem was: on a 10-point sanitization compliance assessment, clinical healthcare professionals average 7.1. The hospital requires an average of at least 9.0.

A goal might be written as: raise sanitization compliance scores from 7.1 to at least 9.0.

That increase would meet the leadership team's requirements and, since the Six Sigma team believes sanitization is related to staph infections, would hopefully improve the overall problem. Understanding how much change the team wants to create in the process will matter for determining the sample size needed for the DOE. The goal needs to be specific enough that the team can use it later to measure success, and it needs to involve the scale of change for the sample-size calculations.

It's worth noting that any given experiment's goal within a Six Sigma project won't be the same as the project's overall initiative. Instead, each experiment goal should relate to — or support — the project's goal. In this case, the team hopes that raising sanitization compliance will help lower staph infection rates.

**Step 3: What's the right Y for your experiment?**

For a designed experiment, you almost always select the output response, or Y, first. The response needs to relate to the overall project goals; since there might be multiple output responses related to the project and the team's experiment goal, the team should ask some questions about the response and possible associated inputs.

- First, is the measurement system capable enough to support the experiment? You can test the measurement system with a gage analysis. The less capable a measurement system is, the larger the sample size and the more experimental runs you'll need. If a measurement system's capability is too poor, then an experiment's time or cost might become prohibitive.
- Second, what's important for the team to address? Does the team want to address variation within a process, or address the process's center? Is the purpose to reduce variation, or move the process mean up or down? In the healthcare scenario presented above, the purpose is to raise the compliance rate.
- The team should also understand how the response might relate to other responses in the process, or whether changes in one response will cause changes in another — particularly if an experiment is being run within a process's live environment. This helps the team manage any downstream changes that might impact other processes or the customer.

The sanitization protocol compliance rate is the Y for the healthcare Six Sigma team's problem.

**Step 4: Which inputs will be studied?**

In the DMAIC chapters, we covered some brainstorming tools for identifying inputs within a process, including the fishbone diagram. More brainstorming tools are covered in Chapter 39. Teams can use those tools, along with process maps, to identify the inputs associated with the outcome decided in the previous step. Once you have a list of inputs, you can select the inputs that will be studied in the experiment. Note that not every input in a process will be studied, and teams should choose inputs that:

- Are considered the most influential on the response (consider the Pareto rule, or 80/20)
- Are quantitative or qualitative in nature (attribute data is harder to work with because of sample-size requirements, and involving many people in the measurement system can also add variation, so keep these considerations in mind)
- Can be properly set and controlled for the experiment

For the healthcare scenario, the team believes several factors might contribute to the lack of compliance: staff training, how long a given team member has been on shift, and the number of patients on the floor at a given time.

**Step 5: What are the factor levels for the experiment?**

At what levels will the input variables be set for the experiment's purposes? If you're running an experiment involving baking cookies, then oven temperature is an input, or factor. The levels for the factor might be 325 degrees F, 350 degrees F, and 375 degrees F. Remember that, in the case of a 2^k factorial, each factor has only two levels.

> **Response, Factor, and Level**
>
> When discussing design of experiments, Six Sigma practitioners might use slightly different terminology to discuss the process components. The response is the process's outcome or output. Factors are the inputs — usually the ones that influence the response and are being studied during the DOE. Levels are the values the factors are set to for the experiment's purposes.
>

In the healthcare example, the team decides to set each factor at a low level and a high level:

- Staff training: received annual compliance refresher training in the last 6 months versus didn't receive the training in the last six months
- Shift time: less than or equal to 4 hours versus 5 or more hours
- Number of patients on the floor: below 80 percent of maximum capacity versus above 80 percent of maximum capacity

The levels set for each factor depend on a variety of considerations. If the team is running a screening experiment — meaning it just wants to test the impact of inputs on outputs or better understand the process — it would set the levels at wide intervals. For optimization, the team likely already has an understanding of the input's impact on the process; the team might have already run analyses or experiments, and that information helps it set the levels appropriately at narrower intervals.

The process itself will dictate how some levels are set. If a Six Sigma team is working with a baking process, for example, it can't set the temperature lower than 0 degrees, and most ovens also have a maximum temperature range. Teams likely also know the temperature around which baked goods will still come out raw, so it's unlikely they'd set temperatures at something like 100 degrees F. Safety should always be a concern when setting levels. An oven might heat up to a maximum of 550 degrees F, but is it safe to try baking cookies at that level?

Finally, the levels need to correlate with the type of information the team is looking for and the size of the change the team wants to see. If a team is working with a manufacturing process that cuts wood, it probably wants to see changes in small increments. Setting the tool's levels several feet apart won't show the change the team wants to see, if they're working with the process of cutting a piece of 2x4 lumber that needs to be cut into 6-inch pieces.

**Step 6: What's the appropriate sample size?**

In the case of design of experiments, a sample size isn't the number of data elements you collect, but the number of times you replicate the experiment. The more replications, the greater the precision of the statistics, but each run in the DOE consumes time and possibly other resources. Six Sigma practitioners have to balance resource use against the need for strong experiment conclusions. When you build a design of experiments in Minitab, the software program generates some predictions about the experiment even before you run it, which lets you decide on size and replication before you start. Specifically, Minitab tells you the effect size, measured in standard deviation, that you have an 80 percent chance of capturing with the experiment as you've designed it.

### Step-by-Step Guide to Running a 2^k Factorial Experiment in Minitab

To learn more about sample size and replication — and how to run a 2^k factorial experiment in Minitab — start with the Assistant menu. You can also access design of experiments under Stat > DOE, but the assistant is useful because it recalls all the steps discussed earlier in this chapter, helps you decide on the right experiment type, and helps you build the data-collection form and the analysis.

For this experiment's setup, use the healthcare example discussed above.

**Problem:** on a 10-point sanitization compliance assessment, clinical healthcare professionals average 7.1. The hospital requires an average of at least 9.0.

**Goal:** raise compliance scores to at least 9.0.

**Response:** compliance rate with sanitization protocols

**Factors:** staff training, shift time, number of patients on the floor

**Levels:**

In the specific healthcare scenario used as an example, running an independent experiment isn't an option — a Six Sigma team isn't going to trigger an infection in patients just to study the inputs. In that case, the team would use historical data that already matches the experiment's parameters (an option, or sometimes a requirement, in various scenarios).

After reviewing Minitab's notes, click "Back" and select "Create Modeling Design."

Minitab displays a Modeling Design dialog box, asking for all the information needed to build an experiment. Enter the information for the healthcare scenario.

1. Name the response variable. The team is measuring compliance with sanitization protocols, so name it "Compliance." The name doesn't matter to Minitab, so you can name the variable whatever makes sense to you or the Six Sigma team.
2. Choose an option for the response goal. Minitab lets you select minimize the response, maximize the response, or hit a target. In this case, the team wants to improve compliance to a score of 9, but going above 9 would also be a positive outcome, so select "maximize the response."
3. Enter the number of factors. Remember, factors are inputs, and the healthcare scenario identifies 3 inputs.
4. Enter names and information for the factors. Even though some of the factors are continuous in nature, since this is a 2^k factorial experiment, we split them into categories.
5. Select a number of times to replicate the experiment (remember, this is relevant to sample size). For this purpose, select 2.
6. Make sure your dialog box matches the one shown below and select OK.

Minitab asks whether you want to print the data-collection form; for this example, select "No."

Minitab generates three items. The first is a modeling design report card, providing next steps and tips for completing the experiment.

> **Create Modeling Design — Report Card**
>
> **Randomization:** when you build a modeling design, Minitab automatically randomizes the order of the experimental runs. Randomization balances the effect of uncontrollable conditions, such as changes in materials or staffing, and reduces the chance those conditions skew the results. When running the modeling experiment, make sure to carry out the runs in the random order specified on the worksheet.
>
> **Replicate versus Repeat:** replicate and repeat measurements are both taken at the same factor settings, but replicates are taken during separate experimental runs, while repeats are taken during the same run. When you add replicates to a design, you take all the runs from the original design and run them again.
>
> **Next Steps:**
> 1. Complete all pre-experiment activities. For more information, see the Pre-Experiment Checklist.
> 2. Run your experiment in the order specified on the worksheet and collect the response data. Make sure to carry out every run in each block under similar conditions.
> 3. Enter the response data in column C8.
> 4. Fit the linear model.
>

The second item is a summary report. The report summarizes all the information you entered for the experiment and provides an estimated detection ability, which helps you choose a sample size.

> **Create Modeling Design — Summary Report**
>
> Design Information: Response Compliance, Goal Maximize, Base design 3 factors / 8 runs, Replicates 2, Center points 0, Total runs 16.
>
> Factors and Settings: StaffEd (No / Yes), TimeShift (4 or under / Over 4), NoPts (Below 80% / 80% or more).
>
> Effect Estimation: this design will estimate all linear main effects and two-way interactions. Replicates are placed in separate blocks.
>
> Experimental Goal: build a model that describes the relationship between the response and the critical factors. If the model is adequate, use it to find the optimal factor settings.
>

The third item is the worksheet to help you gather the experiment's results. Minitab randomizes the run order, which would be necessary if you were completing the experiment in real time.

To make the best possible choice about sample size, it helps to know the current standard deviation, to understand which measurement will be meaningful. Remember, two replicates have an 80 percent chance of detecting 1.36 standard deviations, not a deviation of 1.36 in the actual compliance score.

Before moving forward with the experiment, the team might consider some sample data. Here are the sanitization compliance scores from all of a week's clinical audits.

*(Data table: 20 sanitization compliance scores, ranging from 5.1 to 9.1.)*

Copy the data into Excel or Minitab to calculate this data set's standard deviation.

The standard deviation is 1.028.

According to the first summary, based on the 2-replicate setting, the experiment's detection ability is only an 80 percent chance of detecting changes of 1.36 standard deviations. That's too large to make the difference the healthcare team needs to see. With three replicates, the difference sits right at the edge, and, in any other situation, a Six Sigma practitioner would likely prefer to use 4 or more replicates. For this exercise's purposes, we'll stick with 2 replicates for the rest of the example.

On the Report Card screen, select "View the pre-experiment checklist." Minitab provides four important reminders before running the experiment:

- Train the people involved in the experiment;
- Validate the measurement system;
- Check all the design's combinations (make sure they're safe and possible);
- Run test trials before the real experiment.

First, anyone involved in the experiment needs to be properly trained, to remove variation caused by operator error. The individuals involved need to know how to measure the outcome, or response, how to set the factor levels, if that's needed during the experiment, and how to make equipment or process changes between runs to affect the experiment. In the healthcare example we're using, the only training that might be needed is making sure the audit — which applies the compliance score — is conducted correctly. In another situation, though, a team might be running a production process at a manufacturing plant. The team might want to experiment with different materials, different tools, and different operators as part of the experiment, and would have to make sure everyone knew how to use the materials and tools.

Measurement systems need to be validated for both the response and each factor's levels. In our healthcare example, the Six Sigma team should have already validated the measurement system used to assess compliance. They might have used a Gage R&R to determine whether separate auditors, with separate replications, would rate the same situation the same way more than once, for example. Teams should also validate the measurements used to set levels. If a wheel's speed in a manufacturing process needs to be set at 1 rpm, 1.2 rpm, and 1.5 rpm as a factor's levels, then the calibrations for those settings need to be checked.

When running real experiments, Six Sigma teams should review every possible combination in the experiment to make sure they're all safe and possible. Levels perfectly safe or possible for one factor might become unsafe or impossible when combined with another, for example. The team might want to run a few test trials to work out troubleshooting issues in the experiment and finalize the validations before moving on to the actual experiment.

Finally, the team runs the designed experiment according to the random worksheet Minitab built. In the healthcare scenario, the team reviewed last month's data in random order and logged the first data set that fit each experiment scenario. For example, the first run in the list below required that the team member being audited had received compliance training in the last six months, was past the 4th hour of a shift when the audited interaction occurred, and was working at a time when the specific floor was at 80 percent or more capacity. The first score that met those parameters was 7.9. The data-collection results are included below, and you can copy this table into Minitab if you'd like to follow along with the analysis.

*(Data table: 16 experiment runs — StdOrder, RunOrder, CenterPt, Blocks, StaffEd (Yes/No), TimeShift (Over 4/4 or under), NoPts (Below 80%/80% or more), Compliance — with compliance scores between 5.2 and 9.7.)*

To analyze the results, select Assistant → DOE → Analyze and Interpret → Fit Linear Model, and choose the response goal ("Maximize the response," in this case). The assistant follows a decision flow: if curvature is detected in the data, it suggests collecting additional points and fitting a quadratic model before optimizing; otherwise, it goes straight to optimizing the response.

Click OK. Minitab generates five items:

- A report card
- A prediction and optimization report
- A diagnostic report
- An effects report
- A summary report

The report card provides general information about the analysis and some tips for understanding the results. In this case, the report card notes that no unusual data points, or possible outliers, were identified, and that there's only one significant factor in the experiment according to the statistical analysis.

The prediction and optimization report compares the means associated with significant factors and provides an optimized level setting for those factors. In this case, only one factor — whether the team had received compliance training in the last six months — was statistically significant.

*(Minitab "Prediction and Optimization Report" panel: Goal "Maximize Compliance," Solution "Optimal Setting: StaffEd = Yes," Predicted Y = 9.0625, 95% CI (8.3878; 9.7372); table with Level No (N=8, Mean=6.5996) and Yes (N=8, Mean=9.0625).)*

The effects report provides more information about all the factors. At the bottom of the diagram below, you can see the main-effects plots for each factor. The main effect is the difference between the average response at each factor setting. You can see that only a slight difference occurs between the average responses for different amounts of time spent on shift, and almost no difference occurs between the averages of the two settings for the number of patients on the floor. The biggest difference is seen with respect to compliance-training status. The same holds true at the top of the chart, where different factors are plotted together.

<img alt="Gráfico "Main Effects Plot for StaffEd" gerado pelo Minitab, com o intervalo de confiança de 95% para a média de "No" e "Yes", mostrando o intervalo verde (Yes) como a configuração ótima, Predicted Y=9,0625" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:377px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


The summary report provides a Pareto breakdown of influence on the response. In this case, the biggest influence on the compliance number is whether the team received compliance training in the last six months. The next factor is how long the team member had been working that shift. The third most influential factor is a combination of A (staff training) and B (time worked on shift). The number of patients on the floor only ranks fourth in influence.

The summary notes that setting the staff-training factor to Yes — the team member received training in the last 6 months — results in a predicted Y (response) above 9. The summary also notes that this model explains 68.64 percent of the variation.

<img alt="Relatório "Fit Linear Model for Compliance — Effects Report" do Minitab: Interaction Plots for Compliance (grade StaffEd*TimeShift, StaffEd*NoPts, TimeShift*NoPts) e Main Effects Plots for Compliance (StaffEd, TimeShift, NoPts), com fundo cinza indicando termos não significativos removidos do modelo" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

<img alt="Gráfico "Main Effects Plots for Compliance" gerado pelo Minitab (parte inferior do Effects Report): três painéis mostrando o efeito principal de StaffEd, TimeShift e NoPts sobre a Média de Compliance" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


Based on these results, the Six Sigma team might run additional tests and analysis, but it would also likely make a recommendation about providing compliance training to staff. If you remember, the training originally mentioned was an annual training. However, this experiment appears to indicate that training has more impact if team members received it in the last 6 months. The team might recommend that staff receive the training twice a year going forward.

#### Worked example on five fronts: 2³ Factorial with interactions

The 16 real runs from the sanitization experiment (text above) aren't available as text — only the final result (StaffEd=Yes optimal, predicted Y=9.0625, means 6.5996/9.0625, R²=68.64%). To demonstrate the 2³ factorial's **complete mechanics** with 2 replicates (16 runs) and reading interactions — asked for in Section 4.1 — we use an **illustrative** set with the same design (3 factors A/B/C at -1/+1, 2 replicates) and a similar effect pattern (A dominant, B secondary, C weak): means by level of A ≈ 6.56 (−1) and ≈ 9.06 (+1) — very close to the text's 6.5996/9.0625.

**Data (A, B, C, Response), 16 rows:** (-1,-1,-1,6.55) (-1,-1,1,6.42) (-1,1,-1,6.78) (-1,1,1,6.43) (1,-1,-1,8.60) (1,-1,1,8.26) (1,1,-1,9.63) (1,1,1,9.75) (-1,-1,-1,6.43) (-1,-1,1,6.19) (-1,1,-1,6.97) (-1,1,1,6.74) (1,-1,-1,8.74) (1,-1,1,8.28) (1,1,-1,9.60) (1,1,1,9.58)

<img alt="Ilustracao Excel + Power BI (DAX) do exemplo: Fatorial 2³ com interações" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," style="max-width:100%;" />

**Excel 365**: build the design matrix (columns A, B, C at −1/+1) and the interaction columns (A×B, A×C, B×C, A×B×C are just products of the columns), then run **Data → Data Analysis → Regression** with Y=Response and X=all 7 columns (A, B, C, AB, AC, BC, ABC). The multiple-regression coefficients are the estimated effects — but the Analysis ToolPak doesn't build the design itself (generating the balanced -1/+1 matrix) or the effects Pareto chart automatically.

**Power BI (DAX)**: Power BI doesn't design or fit a factorial model with interactions natively in DAX (multiple regression with residual diagnostics is Section 4.3's non-native case). The recommended standard is to calculate the model in Python/R/Minitab and publish the estimated effects for an effects-Pareto chart on the dashboard:

```dax
Efeito A (importado) = 1.2456
Efeito B (importado) = 0.3756
Efeito AB (importado) = 0.2094
Efeito C (importado) = -0.1031
```

```py-r
--- python
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.formula.api import ols
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

dados = [
    (-1,-1,-1,6.55), (-1,-1,1,6.42), (-1,1,-1,6.78), (-1,1,1,6.43),
    (1,-1,-1,8.60), (1,-1,1,8.26), (1,1,-1,9.63), (1,1,1,9.75),
    (-1,-1,-1,6.43), (-1,-1,1,6.19), (-1,1,-1,6.97), (-1,1,1,6.74),
    (1,-1,-1,8.74), (1,-1,1,8.28), (1,1,-1,9.60), (1,1,1,9.58),
]
df = pd.DataFrame(dados, columns=["A", "B", "C", "Y"])

modelo = ols("Y ~ A*B*C", data=df).fit()
print(modelo.summary().tables[1])

print(f"\nMédia A=Baixo(-1): {df[df.A==-1].Y.mean():.4f}")
print(f"Média A=Alto(+1):  {df[df.A==1].Y.mean():.4f}")

efeitos = modelo.params.drop("Intercept").sort_values(key=abs, ascending=True)
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
plt.barh(efeitos.index, efeitos.values, color="#00688f")
plt.title("Efeitos estimados (fatorial 2³)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```py-r
--- python
%%R
A <- rep(c(-1,-1,-1,-1,1,1,1,1), 2)
B <- rep(c(-1,-1,1,1,-1,-1,1,1), 2)
C <- rep(c(-1,1,-1,1,-1,1,-1,1), 2)
Y <- c(6.55,6.42,6.78,6.43,8.60,8.26,9.63,9.75,
       6.43,6.19,6.97,6.74,8.74,8.28,9.60,9.58)

modelo <- lm(Y ~ A*B*C)
print(summary(modelo)$coefficients)

cat(sprintf("\nMedia A=Baixo(-1): %.4f\n", mean(Y[A==-1])))
cat(sprintf("Media A=Alto(+1):  %.4f\n", mean(Y[A==1])))
```

**Minitab** (current version — check minitab.com): **Stat → DOE → Factorial → Create Factorial Design** (2 levels, 3 factors, 2 replicates) to generate the randomized design matrix, then **Stat → DOE → Factorial → Analyze Factorial Design** (or the Assistant, as in the text) to fit the model and automatically generate the effects-Pareto chart and the main-effects/interactions plot — it's the only one of the five tools that builds the balanced design on its own.

*Cross-check note: Python and R converge on exactly the same coefficients — effect of A ≈ 1.246 (the largest, dominant one), B ≈ 0.376, A×B interaction ≈ 0.209 (statistically significant), C ≈ −0.103, other interactions not significant — reproducing the same qualitative pattern as the text (staff training is the dominant factor, followed by shift time, with a relevant interaction between the two). Excel and DAX are checked manually against these coefficients; the numbers aren't the book's original experiment (raw data unavailable as text), they only reproduce the same pattern and the same analysis mechanics.*

### Next Steps

Remember that an experiment usually isn't what solves the big problem a Six Sigma team is working on. It simply helps address one part of a solution to that problem. In the healthcare Six Sigma team's case, recommending additional training might raise sanitization protocol compliance rates, which, in turn, could lower the hospital's staph infection rate. But that's probably not the only root cause the team found, nor the only solution it'll recommend.

After drawing conclusions from experiments, Six Sigma teams need to take steps to validate the results, implement solutions or fold the results into the overall project, and build controls. These steps will be covered in more detail at the end of the next chapter.
